source: FutureSearch-style auto-generated forecasting question set paper (2026), arXiv 2601.22444
finding: Direct test of forecast decomposition in an LLM pipeline. A ReAct agent writes subquestions, a second model forecasts them blind to the parent question, and the parent forecast sees those results. Brier fell.
numbers: 500 random questions. Gemini 3 Pro Brier 0.141 (95% CI 0.122-0.161) without subquestions, 0.132 (0.115-0.149) with. Subquestion version better in 94.4% of 10,000 bootstrap samples.
limits: Gain is 0.009 Brier. CIs overlap. Sub-forecasts came from GPT-5 with more research effort and were run two days later, so extra research and decomposition are mixed. Base rate of YES was 29.2%. Workshop paper.
agent_relevance: Decomposition may give a small gain, and some of it is just more research. Our O3 test must hold search effort equal.

source: FutureSearch-style auto-generated forecasting question set paper (2026), arXiv 2601.22444
finding: The decomposition prompt is a 3-step recipe: split into subquestions, colleagues forecast each without seeing the top question, then the forecaster combines with sub-forecasts as extra input.
numbers: Prompt asks for 3 to 5 subquestions (Appendix A.19, A.19.1).
limits: Combination step is left to the model, not code. No rule for weights.
agent_relevance: Blind sub-forecasting is a cheap way to avoid anchoring on the parent question. Combine in code, not by the model (G5).

source: FutureSearch-style auto-generated forecasting question set paper (2026), arXiv 2601.22444
finding: Model quality ordering held on the benchmark, so the benchmark can show effects of scaffolds.
numbers: Brier: Gemini 3 Pro 0.134, GPT-5 0.149 (research by GPT-5), Gemini 2.5 Flash 0.179. Calibration component 0.013-0.022; refinement 0.063-0.085. Mean forecasts 0.37-0.42 vs base rate 0.292, so a YES bias.
limits: Brier components computed with K=10 bins. This is the model-ladder test, not the decomposition test.
agent_relevance: Compare any decomposition gain to the model-ladder gap. 0.009 is about one fifth of the gap between best and worst model here (0.045).

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: The retrieval step of a strong LLM forecaster uses decomposition: the model writes sub-questions, each becomes a search query, and these are combined with queries made directly from the question.
numbers: Final system Brier .179 vs human crowd .149. Averaging system and crowd beat both in every setting reported. Random baseline .25.
quote: subquestions cover campaign finances, economic indicators, and geopolitical events
limits: Paper does not run an ablation that isolates the sub-question prompt. Gain from decomposition alone is not reported. Best base model GPT-4-1106 Brier .208 in the simple setting.
agent_relevance: Decomposition is used as a coverage tool for search, not as a probability algebra. Election example: direct query finds polls, sub-questions find campaign finance, economy, geopolitics.

source: Halawi, Zhang, Yueh-Han, Steinhardt (2024) Approaching Human-Level Forecasting with Language Models
finding: The prompt for this step says to write sub-questions first, then use them to steer queries (Figure 12b).
numbers: Two query prompts are merged for coverage.
limits: No measured effect of this prompt alone.
agent_relevance: Cheap form of O3: decompose to widen evidence search, then forecast whole.

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: Decomposition makes testable laws: P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B|A). Models often break these laws, and the size of the break predicts Brier score without waiting for resolution.
numbers: Correlation of violation metric with Brier, first dataset: Cond 0.92 (arbitrage) and 0.87 (frequentist); CondCond 0.78 and 0.71; And 0.68 and 0.72; Negation 0.60 and 0.67; Or only 0.14 and 0.24; AndOr 0.20 and 0.25; aggregated 0.62 and 0.85. Second dataset: Cond 0.71 and 0.69.
limits: Correlations over a small set of forecasters. Some checks (Or, ExpEvidence, Negation on second dataset) are weak or negative. Even o1-mini violates checks.
agent_relevance: Chain-rule checks are a free code-level test on our own decompositions: if parts and whole disagree, flag it (G1 signal, G5 code checks).

source: Paleka et al. (2024) Consistency Checks for Language Model Forecasters
finding: ArbitrageForecaster patches a base forecaster by forcing consistency across related questions, as an arbitrage trader would.
numbers: Improvement reported in Section 5 and Appendix F; figure values not extracted in this session.
limits: I read the method and correlation tables, not the Appendix F numbers. Paper says the patched forecaster is not definitionally consistent.
agent_relevance: Consistency repair is a combine step that code can do. Needs a test for real accuracy gain.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models (ICLR)
finding: Explicit decomposition into subproblems solved in order lets models generalize to problems harder than the examples. On the SCAN length split it nearly solved the task.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: standard 16.7, chain of thought 16.2, least-to-most 99.7. text-davinci-002: 6.0, 0.0, 76.0. code-davinci-001: 0.4, 0.0, 60.7. 14 exemplars.
limits: SCAN is synthetic with a clean grammar. Gains are largest where the structure is natural.
agent_relevance: Where structure is crisp, decomposition beats plain chain of thought by a very large margin. Forecasting questions are not crisp.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models (ICLR)
finding: On math and reading, the gain over chain of thought is small or task dependent.
numbers: Table 11, code-davinci-002: GSM8K zero-shot 16.38, standard 17.06, chain of thought 60.87, least-to-most 62.39. DROP non-football: CoT 74.77, L2M 82.45. DROP football: CoT 59.56, L2M 73.42.
limits: Authors say DROP gains are probably because most DROP problems can be trivially decomposed. GSM8K gain is 1.5 points.
agent_relevance: Expect small gains when the model already walks through the steps by itself.

source: Zhou et al. (2023) Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models (ICLR)
finding: Decomposition helps more on longer chains. By number of steps in GSM8K the gain grows.
numbers: GSM8K accuracy L2M vs CoT: 2 steps 74.53 vs 76.68 (CoT better); 3 steps 68.91 vs 67.29; 4 steps 59.73 vs 59.39; 5+ steps 45.23 vs 39.07.
limits: Differences on 3 and 4 steps are tenths of a point.
agent_relevance: Worth it only for deep problems; for shallow ones skip decomposition (cost and error propagation).

source: Press et al. (2023) Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models (Self-Ask)
finding: Models know the parts but fail to compose them. This gap stays near 40% as GPT-3 gets bigger.
numbers: Compositional Celebrities (8.6k 2-hop questions): davinci-002 answers 45.4% of 2-hop questions. Hardest category: 1.2% on 2-hop while answering 80% of the sub-questions. Gap roughly constant near 40% across model sizes.
limits: GPT-3 family only, 2022 models. Dataset is synthetic templates.
agent_relevance: Core argument for O3 on knowledge problems: ask parts separately, then compose.

source: Press et al. (2023) Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models (Self-Ask)
finding: Self-ask: the model writes the next follow-up question, answers it, then continues. Beats plain chain of thought on multi-hop QA, and a search engine can answer the follow-ups.
numbers: Davinci-002 accuracy. Bamboogle (125 questions): direct 17.6, chain of thought 46.4, self-ask 57.6, self-ask plus search 60.0. 2WikiMultiHopQA: 25.4, 29.8, 30.0, 40.1. Musique (2-hop): 5.6, 12.6, 13.8, 15.2.
limits: Text table was garbled in extraction; row pairing is read from column order. Bamboogle graded by authors by hand. Prompt tuned in a few dozen runs on the training set.
agent_relevance: Structured follow-up scaffolding is easy to parse in code and lets a tool answer each part.

source: Press et al. (2023) Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models (Self-Ask)
finding: Confidence in the parts predicts composition success. Low perplexity on the sub-answers means a high composition rate.
numbers: When max perplexity on correct sub-answers is 1.000-1.002, the model gets 81.1% of 2-hop right; when 1.232-6.738, 42.6%.
limits: Needs token probabilities.
agent_relevance: Part-level confidence can gate when to trust the composed answer.

source: Press et al. (2023) Measuring and Narrowing the Compositionality Gap in Language Models (Self-Ask)
finding: Self-ask vs least-to-most under the same setup is a near tie.
numbers: 2WikiMultiHopQA: least-to-most 29.0 acc, self-ask 35.5 acc (844 vs 569 tokens generated). Musique: 16.8 vs 16.3.
limits: Authors' own comparison; prompts differ.
agent_relevance: Format matters less than whether the parts are asked at all.

source: Khot et al. (2023) Decomposed Prompting: A Modular Approach for Solving Complex Tasks (ICLR)
finding: DecomP splits a task into sub-tasks handled by separate prompts, tools or code. Sub-tasks can be split again or replaced by a symbolic function, including a retriever.
numbers: Tasks: kth-letter concatenation, list reversal (recursive splitting, davinci-001), CommaQA-E, and open-domain multi-hop QA on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue with a retrieval module. Exact values are in bar charts; I read the text only.
limits: The chain-of-thought rollout of the decomposed prompt failed because the unrolled prompt became too long. Chart numbers not extracted.
agent_relevance: Direct template for a planner that routes sub-problems to code or search.

source: Khot et al. (2023) Decomposed Prompting: A Modular Approach for Solving Complex Tasks (ICLR)
finding: Decomposition beat plain few-shot chain of thought most clearly on length generalization, where chain of thought did not generalize at all.
numbers: List reversal: base CoT prompt did not generalize to longer lists; decomposed version generalized to 4, 6, 8, 10 items. Retrieval-based multi-hop QA beat no-decomposition baselines in all settings except Codex on HotpotQA (comparable).
limits: Weak model (davinci-001) chosen to show the gap.
agent_relevance: Recursive split works when sub-problems are the same type as the whole.

source: Dua et al. (2022) Successive Prompting for Decomposing Complex Questions
finding: Asking one simple question at a time, answering it, then asking the next, beat chain of thought on DROP in few-shot and fine-tuned settings. A calculator handles symbolic steps.
numbers: Few-shot DROP dev F1: chain of thought 22.7; successive prompting 25.3 without calculator, 27.2 with calculator, up to about 31.9 with synthetic plus DROP demos (table layout garbled; column mapping uncertain). Abstract: 5% absolute F1 over the best same-supervision model.
limits: Text extraction garbled the table. Fine-tuned T5 setting reported separately. Synthetic data from tables.
agent_relevance: Separate decomposition supervision from answering supervision. Put a calculator in the loop for arithmetic.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Divide-or-Conquer? Which Part Should You Distill Your LLM?
finding: Two-stage (decompose, then solve) beats single-stage by a large margin. A small model can be the decomposer with small loss; it cannot be the solver.
numbers: GSM8K EM / DROP F1 / Bamboogle acc. Single-stage GPT 20.32 / 46.51 / 49.6. Two-stage GPT decomposer plus GPT solver 65.13 / 55.73 / 54.4. Vicuna-13B decomposer with GPT solver 62.93 / 47.13 / 48.8. GPT decomposer with Vicuna solver 28.51 / 20.90 / 29.6. Vicuna both 28.13 / 21.29 / 32.8.
limits: Single-stage baseline is weak on GSM8K (20.32), which inflates the gain. Cost: decomposition about 0.13 dollars vs 0.63 for solving on GSM8K with GPT.
agent_relevance: Decomposing is a cheap, general skill; solving needs knowledge. Solver quality matters more than splitter quality.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Divide-or-Conquer? Which Part Should You Distill Your LLM?
finding: A distilled decomposer generalizes across tasks; a distilled solver does not.
numbers: Distilled decomposer SD-T with GPT solver: 67.02 / 55.19 / 52.0. Distilled solver with GPT decomposer: 48.98 / 13.37 / 31.2 (DROP falls from 55.73 to 13.37).
limits: Teacher is GPT; Vicuna-13B students; three tasks.
agent_relevance: One cheap model for splitting is reasonable if the answering model is strong.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting (ACL)
finding: A zero-shot instruction to first plan subtasks, then do them, beats Zero-shot CoT. Detailed instructions (PS+) do better still.
numbers: text-davinci-003 average over 6 math sets: zero-shot CoT 70.4, PS 72.9, PS+ 76.7. GSM8K: 56.4, 58.2, 59.3. MultiArith 83.8, 87.2, 91.8. AQuA 38.9, 42.5, 46.0. CSQA 65.2 vs 71.9; StrategyQA 63.8 vs 65.4. Few-shot manual CoT average 77.6.
limits: GSM8K gain only 2.9 points. Part of the gain is from the detailed rules (extract variables, calculate step by step), not the plan alone.
agent_relevance: Plan-first helps a bit; much of the lift is in checking each step.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Plan-and-Solve Prompting (ACL)
finding: Error taxonomy: of 46 GSM8K problems zero-shot CoT got wrong, planning targets the missing-step class only.
numbers: Calculation errors 7%, missing-step 12%, semantic misunderstanding 27% (of test examples in a 100-problem sample).
limits: Small hand-labelled sample.
agent_relevance: Decomposition addresses one error class; misreading the question needs another fix.

source: Radhakrishnan et al. (2023) Question Decomposition Improves the Faithfulness of Model-Generated Reasoning
finding: Factored decomposition (each subquestion answered in a separate context) gives the most faithful reasoning but lower accuracy. Chain-of-thought decomposition sits between.
numbers: HotpotQA: zero-shot and few-shot 77.0%, factored decomposition 83.0%, CoT decomposition 86.7%, chain of thought 87.3%. Across four tasks, accuracy order: CoT, CoT decomposition, factored, few-shot, zero-shot. Pareto plot accuracy axis runs from 72.8 to about 86.
limits: One RLHF model, four tasks. Faithfulness measured by perturbation and bias tests, with no ground truth. Authors say gains cost accuracy.
agent_relevance: Separate-context sub-answers cut the chance that the model's hidden prior leaks into the parts. Fits G4 and G2.

source: Radhakrishnan et al. (2023) Question Decomposition Improves the Faithfulness of Model-Generated Reasoning
finding: Faithfulness was scored by truncation sensitivity, corruption sensitivity, and accuracy change under a biased context. Decomposition helped on these.
numbers: Overall 0-1 faithfulness score is the average of normalized metrics; factored scores highest. CoT decomposition looked less faithful than CoT on biased-context tests but more faithful on perturbation tests.
limits: Mixed metrics; authors make no claim on order of importance.
agent_relevance: If we want written steps to be the real cause of the answer, ask the parts in separate calls.

source: Lanham et al. (2023) Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
finding: Chain-of-thought text is often not the real cause of the answer, and larger models give less faithful reasoning on most tasks. This is the problem decomposition was proposed to reduce.
numbers: Abstract: dependence on the CoT varies by task; the boost is not due to extra compute or phrasing; larger, more capable models produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks studied.
limits: Abstract and the pointer to decomposition read in detail; body tables not extracted.
agent_relevance: Do not treat model-written reasoning as a record. Use code-checked parts (G2).

source: Kalyan et al. (2021) How Much Coffee Was Consumed During EMNLP 2019? Fermi Problems
finding: Fermi problems are the original estimation form of decomposition. A T5 model fine-tuned on 1k real and 10k synthetic Fermi problems was off by about two orders of magnitude on average.
numbers: Datasets: REALFP 1k, SYNTHFP 10k, with executable programs and facts. Score runs from 1 (exact) to 0 (off by 3 or more orders of magnitude). About 80% of generated programs were syntactically valid; most were single-operation. Outputting and executing the program gave the best score.
limits: T5 fine-tuning, not a modern LLM. Full-setting scores very low (table garbled). Decompositions were seldom meaningful.
agent_relevance: Execute the decomposition in code rather than let the model estimate the total. Check that sub-questions are meaningful.

source: Kalyan et al. (2021) How Much Coffee Was Consumed During EMNLP 2019? Fermi Problems
finding: Two failure patterns: right answer with a meaningless decomposition, and a sound decomposition with a bad sub-estimate far off the truth.
numbers: Examples: 'airborne over Europe' compiled accuracy 0.98 with a meaningless decomposition; 'jelly beans in a bucket' 0.00 with a sound decomposition; another example three orders of magnitude off.
limits: Anecdotal examples from the paper.
agent_relevance: Grade the parts and the whole separately; a right total can hide a wrong path.

source: Karger et al. (2025) ForecastBench: A Dynamic Benchmark of AI Forecasting Capabilities
finding: ForecastBench compares models to humans on future questions. It tests zero-shot, scratchpad, retrieval and crowd-informed prompts. A text search for decomposition or sub-question found no hit.
numbers: Seven baselines: zero-shot, scratchpad, scratchpad with news, zero-shot with crowd, scratchpad with crowd, scratchpad with news and crowd, and an aggregate.
limits: Absence of an arm is not absence of effect.
agent_relevance: Decomposition remains untested on the main public benchmark; our own test adds value.

source: Hsieh et al. (2024) Reasoning and Tools for Human-Level Forecasting
finding: Searched the full text for decomposition or sub-question: no mention. Its agent uses reasoning plus tools, not question splitting.
numbers: No decomposition number reported.
limits: Negative search result only.
agent_relevance: Do not cite as evidence for or against O3.
